div.head: Chapter 3
div.p: The third kind of unbelievers is and are heretics and apostates, who are subjects in law of the universal Church and of its head, who is the vicar of the supreme pontiff and pope, and of the other spiritual prelates. The reason they are subjects is this: by reason of origin, domicile, contract, and by reason of offense, they are subjects both in law and in fact, that is, in act, as those who were born, or whose parents were born, within the dominion of some Christian prince. Others may be subjects only in law and not in fact, that is, in act, as would happen if an entire kingdom with its king, recognizing no temporal superior, were to turn heretic, as did the unfortunate king and kingdom of England and many provinces of Germany. These, then, are subjects of the Church in law by reason of having received the Catholic faith. And the root of this subjection is the solemn vow and the spontaneous profession and promise they made upon receiving holy baptism, by which every baptized person protests and promises to believe in God, Three and One, and to hold the faith of Jesus Christ. This is proved in c. prima, et c. postquam, et c. primum interrogatur, et postquam vos, et c. cathecumenum. de consecratione. dist. 4.

Likewise, the baptized person binds himself by stipulation. Stipulation is when one responds by conceding and promising what the other asks or demands, as in saying: do you promise? — I promise, and the like, according to the jurists. Thus the priest asks the one about to be baptized: Do you believe in God? — He answers: I believe. Do you renounce Satan? — I renounce him, etc. And that exchange is an instance of stipulation, and thus a contract or quasi-contract intervenes between the priest as a public person and minister of the Church, and the one being baptized.

Likewise, the baptized person, by the said contract and by the said acts, promises implicitly and tacitly his obedience, and transfers himself to the dominion, vassalage, and jurisdiction of Jesus Christ and of his Church, setting aside, fleeing, and renouncing the lordship of the first lord, who is the devil, who held him in his power, in order from that point forward to live according to the divine evangelical law, and thus to be numbered and joined in the assembly of Christians, which is the universal Church, outside of which no salvation of the soul is or will be found, as in c. postquam se baptizatus et c. ante baptismum in fi. et c. ab antiqua et c. postquam ascendit. et c. nullius, De consecratione, dist. 4. It is manifest that every subject is bound to live according to the laws of the one to whose principality he submitted himself, as in Codex, De summa Trinitate, L. cunctos populos. et cap. 1 De constitutionibus and cap. fi. de foro competenti.

Since heretics and apostates were subjects of Christ in a certain new way, and of his Church as citizens of the Christian commonwealth, by abandoning the Catholic faith or by violating it with errors, they break their vow and fail to honor the contract concluded by stipulation. Likewise they make themselves disobedient to the laws of Christ and of his Christian commonwealth, and in all of this they commit most grievous offenses and sins and the crime of lèse-majesté. Therefore the Church justly punishes and chastises them, depriving them by operation of law or by deed itself of all their temporal and spiritual goods: of their states, honors, dignities, of all lordship and royal or imperial jurisdiction, as appears from cap. cum secundum leges, De hereticis. Lib. 6 et in cap. vergentis et cap. excomunicamus, el 1.º, 1, Extra., eo. tit. et Codex, De hereticis, L. 4, and in many other places, and the many other penalties that both bodies of law impose on heretics. And thus they are incapable of all jurisdiction: c. quicumque hereticos, eo. tit., Lib. 6 and St. Thomas 2.2, q. 12, a. 2 in the body of the article. And thus the kingdoms of heretics are said to be vacant, and as things that have no owner, the pope is accustomed and able to grant them to some Christian king to occupy and possess as his own, as throughout the title De hereticis, presertim in d. cap. excomunicamus, § moneantur et in cap. presidentes, et in cap. acusatus, § seculares potestates, et in cap. statutum, el 1, et cap. ut inquisitionis, eo. titulo, Lib. 6, etc.
